116	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
117	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
118	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
119	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
120	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
121	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
122	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
123	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
124	
125	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
126	
127	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
128	
129	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
130	
131	## Writing to the record
132	
133	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
134	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
135	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
136	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
137	  - what it means for the work;
138	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
139	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
140	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
141	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
142	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
143	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
144	
145	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
146	
147	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
148	
149	To add a row:
150	
151	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
152	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
153	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
154	
155	To change a row:
156	
157	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters.
158	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
159	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
160	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
161	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.
162	
163	## The repository's history
164	
165	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
166	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
167	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
168	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
169	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
170	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.
171	# The gate
172	
173	The gate runs the seven steps below on one tree, in about 25 minutes. It is green if every step passes, and red if one fails. If a step fails, run the rest, so that the summary holds every step's result.
174	
175	## What it writes
176	
177	The summary, `summary.txt`, has one tab-separated row for each suite: `track/suite`, tests, failures, errors, skipped. Below the rows, lines that start with `#` give each log's `BUILD` and `Total time:` lines, the machine that ran the gate (`# machine`), the atomic runs and the ladder's comparison. A landed summary can also end with `# microgpt-walk` lines: the `VERDICT:` and `rc=` lines of the microGPT walk check (`interpreter.md`, "The model program"), run on the landed tree. Add them only if your brief asks for the microGPT walk check on the landed tree.
178	
179	If your brief asks you to land a gate's results, put them in a new `gate/` folder in `explorations/compile-ladder/`, under the `climb-batch-` name that your brief gives, in the form of the newest one: `summary.txt`, and in `ladder/` the files `ladder.tsv`, `microgpt-phase.md`, `comparison.txt` and `microgpt-comparison.txt`. The next gate compares with the newest summary there or in `explorations/compile-ladder/gate-baseline/`, and finds no other. Land them in a commit that changes nothing else that the gate reads.
180	
181	Steps 5 and 7 use shell functions that `explorations/coordinator/tools/gate-functions.sh` defines. The file runs nothing. In each Bash call of steps 5 and 7, set up the call as `build-and-caches.md` says, which sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the tree's root. Then source the file, from the root:
182	
183	    source explorations/coordinator/tools/gate-functions.sh
184	
185	## When to run it
186	
187	Your brief says whether you run the gate. If it does not ask, run only your own tests (`tests-running.md`).
188	
189	If it asks, first check whether the newest gate still holds for your tree. A gate's tables stay valid until the tree changes under `ProjectFortress/` or `Library/`, or in `build.xml`, outside the test files. A test file is a `.fss`, `.fsi` or `.test` file directly in `ProjectFortress/tests/` or a `ProjectFortress/*_tests/` directory. The commit that landed the newest summary changed nothing that the gate reads. Commit your tree, then run this command. It prints each path, test files excepted, changed since that commit:
190	
191	    G=$(git log -1 --format=%H -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt')
192	    git diff --name-only $G HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library build.xml \
193	        | grep -v -E '^ProjectFortress/([^/]*_)?tests/[^/]*\.(fss|fsi|test)$'
194	
195	- If it prints a path, run the gate.
196	- If not, the newest gate holds. Run only the changed test files, through `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` (`tests-running.md`).
197	
198	## The steps
199	
200	Run these steps from the tree's root. Keep the logs of steps 2 and 4 in `tmp/gate/`, as `compileAll.txt`, `testFast.txt`, `testSystem.txt` and `testSpecData.txt`.
201	
202	1. Read the Avail column of `df -h /`. Warning: deleting `/tmp/fortress*rats` can break other live runs. If the column shows less than 1 GB, delete `/tmp/fortress*rats`, `ProjectFortress/test-tmp` and `ProjectFortress/test-caches`, and read it again. If it still shows less than 500 MB, stop and report.
203	2. Run `rm -rf ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS tmp/gate && mkdir -p tmp/gate`, then `ant compileAll`.
204	3. If the build printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, run the library order (`build-and-caches.md`). If not, and a source of the compiler's library changed since the caches were filled, take its step in `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library". Then copy the caches twice for the ladder regression, before anything else compiles into them:
205	
206	       D=$PWD/tmp/gate/ladder ; mkdir -p $D/root
207	       cp -a default_repository/caches $D/root/ladder-caches
208	       cp -a default_repository/caches $D/root/pristine
209	
210	4. Run `ant testFast`, then `ant testSystem`, then `ant testSpecData`. All three must have zero failures.
211	5. Write the summary: `gate_summary tmp/gate tmp/gate/summary.txt`. Compare it: `gate_compare "$(last_landed_summary)" tmp/gate/summary.txt`. It prints a line for a suite with failures or errors, a suite with no tests, a suite whose count of tests fell, and a suite that is gone. Each such line makes the gate red. A count that rose prints nothing.
212	6. Do the atomic runs, and append their lines to the summary.
213	7. Do the ladder regression.
214	
215	## The atomic runs
216	
217	The atomic runs compile fourteen programs, and run each one three times at four threads, in about a minute. They need the library's jars in the tree's caches (`build-and-caches.md`). Run them from `ProjectFortress/`:
218	
219	    for p in AtomicTopLevelObjectVar AtomicTopLevelVar MutableTopLevelVarInLoop FirstLoadThreadsRungG \
220	             atomic0 atomic1 atomic2 atomic3 atomic4 atomic5 atomic6 \
221	             nestedTransactions0 nestedTransactions1 nestedTransactions2 ; do
222	      d=other_compiler_tests ; [ -f compiler_tests/$p.fss ] && d=compiler_tests
223	      timeout -k 5 300 ../bin/fortress compile $d/$p.fss >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "# atomic $p COMPILE-FAILED" ; continue ; }
224	      for i in 1 2 3 ; do
225	        out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$?
226	        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && { out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$? ; }
227	        case "$out" in *FAIL*) r=FAIL ;; *PASS*) r=PASS ;; *) r="NO-PASS rc=$rc" ;; esac
228	        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && r=TIMEOUT-TWICE
229	        echo "# atomic $p run$i threads=4 $r"
230	      done
231	    done
232	
233	The gate is red on any FAIL, NO-PASS, COMPILE-FAILED or TIMEOUT-TWICE.
234	
235	## The ladder regression
236	
237	The compile ladder records how far each test program gets through the compiler's phases, in order: parse, disambiguate, typecheck, codegen, link, run and pass. The ladder regression runs part of it again, and compares the result with the baseline, `explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/`:
238	
239	- It compiles and runs the 85 programs of the baseline's `pass-list.txt`. It compares each one's phase and output with the baseline's `raw/`.
240	- It compiles the eighteen components of the two microGPT programs, and never runs them. It compares each one's phase with the baseline's `microgpt-phase.md`.
241	
242	A file that moved gets a mark:
243	
244	- DOWN: a phase lower than the record.
245	- MISSING: a file with no output.
246	- STDOUT: output that differs from the record after the `Operation took <n>ms` line is masked.
247	- UP: a phase higher than the record. This is progress, not red.
248	
249	DOWN, MISSING and STDOUT are red, unless your brief declared that move as expected before the gate ran.
250	Warning: do not run `run-ladder.sh`, the driver over every test program, with its defaults. Its default root is shared, its cache pruning corrupts a parallel run, and its default `OUT` is a tracked folder.
251	
252	To run it, as step 7, with step 3's copies of the caches:
253	
254	1. Copy the drivers into `tmp/gate/ladder/`, and point their outputs and caches there:
255	
256	       D=$PWD/tmp/gate/ladder ; B=explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19
257	       cp explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/run-subset.sh \
258	          $B/classify.py $B/microgpt-phase.sh $B/microgpt-phase.py $D/
259	       sed -i -e "s|^OUT=.*|OUT=$D|" -e "s|^LADDER_ROOT=.*|LADDER_ROOT=$D/root|" $D/run-subset.sh
260	       sed -i -e "s|/home/user/fortress|$PWD|g" \
261	           -e "s|^export LADDER_CACHES=.*|export LADDER_CACHES=$D/root/ladder-caches|" \
262	           -e "s|^export LADDER_TMP=.*|export LADDER_TMP=$D/root/ladder-tmp|" \
263	           -e "s|^RAW=.*|RAW=$D/raw/microgpt|" -e "s|^TSV=.*|TSV=$D/microgpt-results.tsv|" $D/microgpt-phase.sh
264	       tail -n +2 $B/pass-list.txt | cut -f1 | sed 's|/|\t|' > $D/subset.txt
265	
266	2. Run the four scripts, with no arguments, in this order: `bash $D/run-subset.sh`, `python3 $D/classify.py`, `bash $D/microgpt-phase.sh` and `python3 $D/microgpt-phase.py`. Each reads and writes in `$D`. This takes about 200 s for the 85 and 35 s for the eighteen, so run them in the background (`session.md`, "Long commands"). With step 3's copies, the driver skips the library's build (about 145 s).
267	3. Compare: `ladder_compare $B $D`, then `diff <(mg_phases $B/microgpt-phase.md) <(mg_phases $D/microgpt-phase.md)`. Append each line that they print to the summary, with `# ladder ` before it.
268	
269	If your brief asks for your change's own ladder subset, write your own `subset.txt`. Put in it each file whose recorded first error in the baseline's `raw/` names something that your change touched. Run them after your edit only. Compare them with the newest landed `ladder.tsv`, or with the baseline's `raw/` for a file that the gate does not run.
270	
271	## Comparing with an earlier run
272	
273	- `ant testSystem` runs in four shards, the summary's rows `system-0` to `system-3`. A shard takes the files by their place in a sorted list, so an added file moves every later file to another shard. When you compare by hand, compare only the sum of the four. `gate_compare` sums them.
274	- In printed output, mask only these differences: the `Operation took <n>ms` line, a Java line number in a stack frame, an object's identity hash (`@` and hex digits), and a position in a library file that your change moved. In your report, list each test with a masked difference, and the kinds masked in it.
275	- If your brief asks you to compare the interpreter tests with a base run, use the two scripts in `explorations/coordinator/tools/count-run/`. `count-run.sh` runs every `ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss` under walk, one JVM per test: run it once on the base commit and once after your edit. `compare-normalised.py` compares the two runs, with the last three masks above. Each script's header gives its usage.
276	# The specification
277	
278	Three folders hold the team's specification:
279	
280	- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
281	- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
282	- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.
283	
284	Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.
285	
286	A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.
287	
288	The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.
289	
290	To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".
291	
292	## Changing the text: the revision form
293	
294	Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.
295	
296	1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
297	   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
298	   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
299	   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
300	   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.
301	
302	   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.
303	
304	2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:
305	
306	       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}
307	
308	   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.
309	
310	3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.
311	
312	4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.
313	
314	If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.
315	
316	Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.
317	
318	## Building it
319	
320	To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):
321	
322	    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &
323	
324	- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'Reference .* undefined\|multiply defined\|Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
325	- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.
326	- The build writes only ignored files, its log among them, which can reach 400 MB. Remove them afterwards: `git clean -fXq -- Specification`.
327	- Update `Specification/fortress.pdf` only if your brief asks for it: copy `Specification/fortress/fortress.pdf` over it.
328	
329	## When the text and an implementation disagree
330	
331	- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, the other side is wrong. If the wrong side is in your area, change it to agree. If not, record the departure as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says.
332	- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
333	- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds.
334	
335	## Citing it
336	
337	- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
338	- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.
339

== Specification/basic/expressions/reductions.tex:12-131

\section{Summations and Other Reduction Expressions}
\seclabel{reduction-expr}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{FlowExpr} &::=&
\emph{Accumulator} \option{\emph{StaticArgs}}
\options{\texttt[ \emph{GeneratorClauseList} \texttt]} \emph{Expr} \\

\emph{Accumulator} &::=& $\sum$ $|$ $\prod$ $|$ \KWD{BIG} (\emph{Encloser} $|$ \emph{Op})
\end{Grammar}

A \emph{reduction expression} begins with a big operator such as
$\sum$ or $\prod$ followed by an optional static arguments and
an optional generator clause list (described in
\secref{generators}), followed by a body expression.
\revision{revival-reductions}{The desugaring of a reduction is directed by
type in this specification: a sum is desugared with the reduction for the type
\VAR{N} of the expression (\secref{desugaring-generators}).
Neither implementation directs it by the type \VAR{N} of the expression yet.
When no argument of the big operator fixes the element type, the interpreter,
which has no static types, directs it by run-time types
(\secref{static-arg-inference}): it instantiates the big operator by the
declared type of the local variable, or the declared return type of the
top-level or local function, whose value the reduction is, where that type
fixes the operator's result type, and otherwise by the join of
the run-time types of the reduction's elements, or, where there is no element,
at the bound of the big operator's static parameter, or open where that bound
mentions the static parameter itself, as the bounds of $\sum$, $\prod$ and
\EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\OPR{MIN}} do; so an empty reduction that no declared type
directs takes the identity of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} whatever the type of the
expression (row~716 of the revival's gap ledger); the compiled type
checker, when it checks the libraries
this specification describes, takes the bound of the big operator's static
parameter, which is not the element type, or, where the reduction's type at
that bound does not fit the reduction's expected type, that expected type
(\secref{static-arg-inference}): a bound such as \TYP{Number} gives the
reduction that type where it has no expected type, and a bound that mentions
the static parameter itself gives no instance that applies, so that the
reduction is refused (row~425).
Until the compiled type checker directs the desugaring by type, a reduction
with a generator clause list whose element type no argument fixes writes its
static argument in a program that both implementations are to run, as the
team's own tests do, as in
\EXP{\sum\llbracket\mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket [j \gets 0\#i]\: f(j)};
a reduction without a generator clause list, such as \EXP{\sum a}, needs none.
Until the compiled path is built on those libraries, it compiles against a
smaller library of its own, whose big operators $\sum$ and
\EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\OPR{MAX}} take no static argument and range over
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} only; there the clause form runs without its static
argument, and a written static argument is refused.
The normative text is unchanged.}
There is no explicit relationship between \EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\emph{Op}} and
\emph{Op}.  Instead, a reduction expression corresponds to a call to the
\EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\emph{Op}} operator, which has the following header:
%% opr BIG Op[\T\](g:(Reduction[\R0\],T->R0)->R0):R
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{BIG}}\: \emph{Op}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(g\COLONOP(\TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket,T\rightarrow{}R_{0})\rightarrow{}R_{0})\COLONOP{}R\)
\end{Fortress}
Here \VAR{R} is the result type of the operator, and \VAR{g} corresponds to
the method %generate[\R0\]
\EXP{\VAR{generate}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket}
of the trait %Generator[\T\]
\EXP{\TYP{Generator}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}:
it is a function that takes a reduction (of type %Reduction[\R0\]
\EXP{\TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket})
and a body (of type \EXP{T\rightarrow{}R_{0}})
and returns a value of type \EXP{R_{0}} by running body on each
generated element and combining them using the reduction.
When a generator clause
list is provided, generator clauses produce values and bind the values to the
identifiers that are used in the subexpression.  Each iteration of the
body expression is assumed to be evaluated in a separate implicit
thread as described in \secref{generators}.  The resulting values are
combined together using \emph{Op}
\label{redexpr-redvar}
as with reduction variables (see \secref{reduction-vars}).
The value of a reduction expression is this combined value.
When no generator clause list is provided, the body is taken to be an
object of type \TYP{Generator} and the elements it generates are
combined.  Thus, the reduction expression \EXP{\sum a} is equivalent
to \EXP{\sum\limits_{x\leftarrow{}a}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu{x}}.

A reduction expression with a generator list:
%% \sum [v_1 \gets g_1, v_2 \gets g_2, \ldots] e
\begin{Fortress}
\(\sum [v_{\mathrm{1}} \gets g_{\mathrm{1}}, v_{\mathrm{2}} \gets g_{\mathrm{2}}, \ldots] e\)
\end{Fortress}
is equivalent to the following code:
%do
%  var result: ZZ32 = 0
%  for v1 <- g1, v2 <- g2, \ldots do
%    result += e
%  end
%  result
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{do}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{var}\:\VAR{result}\COLON \mathbb{Z}32 = 0\)\\
\(  \KWD{for}\:v_{1} \leftarrow g_{1}, v_{2} \leftarrow g_{2}, \ldots \KWD{do}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \VAR{result} \mathrel{+}= e\)\-\\\poptabs
\(  \KWD{end}\)\\
\(  \VAR{result}\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
where \VAR{result} is a fresh variable.
%
A reduction expression without a generator clause list:
%% \sum g
\begin{Fortress}
\(\sum g\)
\end{Fortress}
is equivalent to the following:
%\sum [x \gets g] x
\begin{Fortress}
\(\sum [x \gets g] x\)
\end{Fortress}
Note that reduction expressions without generator clause lists can be used to
conveniently sum any aggregate expression (described in
\secref{aggregate-expr}), since every aggregate expression
is a generator.

**Primer.** An api lists what a component offers. Writing `abstract` on a member in the api says that the component's trait leaves it without a body, so each object below the trait gives it one:

    (* api *)        trait String ... abstract balanced(): String ... end
    (* component *)  trait String ... end                     (* no balanced at all *)
    (* component *)  object FlatString ... balanced(): String = self end

Under the landed reading, this pair matches. Under the other, the component's trait must declare `balanced` too, with or without a body.

**The team's word.** `Specification/basic/components/apis.tex:252-256`: "A matching definition of a declaration $d$ is a definition $d'$ with the same name as $d$ that includes definitions for all declarations other than the methods or fields declared abstract in $d$." `Specification/basic/components/source-code.tex:384-385` lets a satisfying trait "provide a concrete declaration" of an abstract method, which reads as still declaring it (row 816's notes).

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## Landed semantics

FACTS.md:175
- F-228 **Under walk, a reduction or a comprehension that writes no static argument instantiates its big operator by a declared type, else by the join of its elements' run-time types, else at its bound, where an F-bounded parameter stays open.** It builds P-48. The declared type is a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's declared return type, for either also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a top-level variable, a field, an assignment, a function expression, a branch, a call's argument and another clause form's body do not direct it. Otherwise the clauses run once into the library's collector, `__elemsOf`, which keeps the elements in order, typed at the join of their run-time types, and the operator is instantiated at that join; the reduction then runs over the collected elements, so each body runs once. A declared type or a join that does not fit falls back to the instance that no hint gives: a plain-bounded parameter takes its bound, and an F-bounded one stays open (F-143). So a `SUM` of `ZZ32` and `RR64` values, whose join `Number` is outside the bound, runs with each `+` at its operands' types. The same holds with no element and no declared type. With the big operator so instantiated, the library types `__bigOperator`'s local function `body(i: I)` at the element type `I`. A big operator whose declared result is a trait of its own is read through the `BigReduction`, `Comprehension` or `BigOperator` that the trait extends (row 718, fixed). Still wrong, each a ledger row: an empty clause form that no declared type directs takes its bound or stays open (row 716); a comprehension that no declared type reaches is built at its elements' run-time class, as `ArrayList[\Int\]`, which a declared `List[\ZZ32\]` refuses (rows 20, 717); a clause form that is a call's argument gets no declared type (rows 510, 705). Gated by `tests/UnwrittenListMapComprehensionWalk`, `UnwrittenComprehension*Walk`, `ComprehensionTypedBindingWalk`, `UnwrittenSetBigOperatorsWalk`, `UnwrittenEmptyFloatSumWalk`, `IntMapComprehensionTypedWalk` and `UserBigOperatorResultTraitWalk`. component NestedReductionFusion
import List.{...}
import Generator2.{...}
export Executable

(* A reduction of reductions over the prefixes of a list answers the same with and without fusion, whether or not the inner reduction distributes over the outer one. *)

sumSum(gg: Generator[\Generator[\ZZ32\]\]): ZZ32 =
    __bigOperator2[\ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,Generator[\ZZ32\]\](
        SUM[\ZZ32\](), SUM[\ZZ32\](), gg, fn (x: ZZ32): ZZ32 => x)

maxMax(gg: Generator[\Generator[\ZZ32\]\]): ZZ32 =
    __bigOperator2[\ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,Maybe[\ZZ32\],ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,Maybe[\ZZ32\],ZZ32,Generator[\ZZ32\]\](
        BIG MAX[\ZZ32\](), BIG MAX[\ZZ32\](), gg, fn (x: ZZ32): ZZ32 => x)

maxSum(gg: Generator[\Generator[\ZZ32\]\]): ZZ32 =
    __bigOperator2[\ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,Maybe[\ZZ32\],ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,Generator[\ZZ32\]\](
        BIG MAX[\ZZ32\](), SUM[\ZZ32\](), gg, fn (x: ZZ32): ZZ32 => x)

minSum(gg: Generator[\Generator[\ZZ32\]\]): ZZ32 =
    __bigOperator2[\ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,Maybe[\ZZ32\],ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,Generator[\ZZ32\]\](
        BIG MIN[\ZZ32\](), SUM[\ZZ32\](), gg, fn (x: ZZ32): ZZ32 => x)

sumProd(gg: Generator[\Generator[\ZZ32\]\]): ZZ32 =
    __bigOperator2[\ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,Generator[\ZZ32\]\](
        SUM[\ZZ32\](), PROD[\ZZ32\](), gg, fn (x: ZZ32): ZZ32 => x)

unfused(f: Generator[\Generator[\ZZ32\]\] -> ZZ32, gg: Generator[\Generator[\ZZ32\]\]): ZZ32 = do
    switchDispatching(false)
    r = f(gg)
    switchDispatching(true)
    r
end

run(): () = do
    l = <|[\ZZ32\] 1, 3, 2 |>
    assert(unfused(sumSum, inits l), 11, "the sum of the prefix sums of 1, 3, 2 without fusion is 11")
    assert(sumSum(inits l), 11, "the sum of the prefix sums of 1, 3, 2 is 11; a sum does not distribute over a sum")
    assert(unfused(maxMax, inits l), 3, "the maximum of the prefix maxima of 1, 3, 2 without fusion is 3")
    assert(maxMax(inits l), 3, "the maximum of the prefix maxima of 1, 3, 2 is 3; a maximum does not distribute over a maximum")
    assert(unfused(maxSum, inits l), 6, "the maximum prefix sum of 1, 3, 2 without fusion is 6")
    assert(maxSum(inits l), 6, "the maximum prefix sum of 1, 3, 2 is 6")
    assert(unfused(minSum, inits l), 1, "the minimum prefix sum of 1, 3, 2 without fusion is 1")
    assert(minSum(inits l), 1, "the minimum prefix sum of 1, 3, 2 is 1")
    assert(unfused(sumProd, inits l), 10, "the sum of the prefix products of 1, 3, 2 without fusion is 10")
    assert(sumProd(inits l), 10, "the sum of the prefix products of 1, 3, 2 is 10")
    println("PASS")
  end

end
(* The generator, condition, reduction and generator-of-generators declarations whose static arguments and declared types the compiled checker refused, called under walk with the values they answer. *)
component GeneratorDeclarations
import List.{...}
import Generator2.{...}
export Executable

inOrder[\E\](g: Generator[\E\]): String = do
    s: String := ""
    for x <- seq(g) do s := s || x || "," end
    s
end

fusedMax(gg: Generator[\Generator[\ZZ32\]\]): ZZ32 =
    __bigOperator2[\ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,Maybe[\ZZ32\],ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,Generator[\ZZ32\]\](
        BIG MAX[\ZZ32\](), SUM[\ZZ32\](), gg, fn (x: ZZ32): ZZ32 => x)

naiveMax(gg: Generator[\Generator[\ZZ32\]\]): ZZ32 = do
    switchDispatching(false)
    r = fusedMax(gg)
    switchDispatching(true)
    r
end

run() = do
    yes: Boolean = (1 < 2)
    no: Boolean = (2 < 1)
    none = NoReductionPair[\ZZ32\]
    some = SumReduction[\ZZ32\].distribute(MaxReduction[\ZZ32\])

    assert(yes.cond[\ZZ32\](fn (): ZZ32 => 1, fn (): ZZ32 => 2), 1, "a condition that holds runs its first branch")
    assert(no.cond[\ZZ32\](fn (): ZZ32 => 1, fn (): ZZ32 => 2), 2, "a condition that does not hold runs its second branch")
    assert(inOrder(yes.indexValuePairs), "(0,()),", "a condition that holds pairs its one element with index 0")
    assert(inOrder(no.indexValuePairs), "", "a condition that does not hold has no index-value pairs")
    assert(inOrder(none.indexValuePairs), "", "the empty reduction pair has no index-value pairs")
    assert(yes.ivmap[\ZZ32\](fn (i: ZZ32, u: ()): ZZ32 => i + 7).asString, "Just(7)", "a condition that holds, mapped with its index 0 by adding 7, is Just(7)")
    assert(no.ivmap[\ZZ32\](fn (i: ZZ32, u: ()): ZZ32 => i + 7).asString, "Nothing", "a condition that does not hold, mapped with its index, is Nothing")
    assert(none.ivmap[\ZZ32\](fn (i: ZZ32, p: Any): ZZ32 => 5).asString, "Nothing", "the empty reduction pair mapped with its index is Nothing")
    assert(some.ivmap[\ZZ32\](fn (i: ZZ32, p: Any): ZZ32 => i + 5).asString, "Just(5)", "a reduction pair mapped with its index 0 by adding 5 is Just(5)")
    assert(none.map[\ZZ32\](fn (p: Any): ZZ32 => 5).asString, "Nothing", "the empty reduction pair mapped is Nothing")
    assert(some.map[\ZZ32\](fn (p: Any): ZZ32 => 5).asString, "Just(5)", "a reduction pair mapped to 5 is Just(5)")

component InferUnfixedFBoundedWalk
import Set.{...}
export Executable

(* A type parameter whose bound mentions itself and that nothing at a call fixes is left open under walk: every value is admitted where its type is expected, so a reduction with no static argument runs on its elements' own types. *)

trait Cmp[\T\] end

object BoxU[\T\]()
    getter kind(): String = "boxed"
end

mk[\T extends Cmp[\T\]\](): BoxU[\T\] = BoxU[\T\]()

run(): () = do
    r = SUM[j <- 0#4] (j / 2.0)
    assert(r, 3.0, "a sum of RR64 elements with no static argument joins its elements with their own + (reductions.tex, section \"Summations and Other Reduction Expressions\")")
    p = PROD[j <- 1#0] j
    assert(p, 1, "an empty product of ZZ32 elements with no static argument is the identity 1 (reductions.tex, section \"Summations and Other Reduction Expressions\")")
    lo = BIG MIN[j <- 0#4] (j - 2)
    assert(lo, -2, "BIG MIN with no static argument over j - 2 for j in 0#4 is -2 (reductions.tex, section \"Summations and Other Reduction Expressions\")")
    hi = BIG MAX[j <- 0#4] (j - 2)
    assert(hi, 1, "BIG MAX with no static argument over j - 2 for j in 0#4 is 1 (reductions.tex, section \"Summations and Other Reduction Expressions\")")
    s = { n^2 | n <- -2:2 }
    assert(|s|, 3, "a set comprehension with no static argument over n^2 for n in -2:2 holds three elements (comprehensions.tex, section \"Comprehensions\")")
    assert((0 IN s) AND (1 IN s) AND (4 IN s), true, "the set comprehension over n^2 for n in -2:2 holds 0, 1 and 4 (comprehensions.tex, section \"Comprehensions\")")
    b = mk()
    assert(b.kind, "boxed", "a call that fixes no static argument of a function whose type parameter's bound mentions itself runs, and its result answers its getter (inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\")")
    assert("ab.c".upto('.'), "ab", "String's upto, whose body calls BIG MIN with no static argument, answers the prefix before the character")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

\subsection{List Expressions}
\seclabel{list-expr}

List element expressions are enclosed in
angle brackets $\llbracket$ and $\rrbracket$ and are separated by commas.
The type of a list expression is \EXP{\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
 where \VAR{T}
is the union type of the types of all element expressions.

A list \VAR{l} is indexed by placing an index enclosed in square brackets
immediately after an expression evaluating to \VAR{l}.
\marginnote{The new fortify fixes this.}
Thus, the index is rendered as a subscript.
Lists are always indexed from \EXP{0}.
For example:
2503-
2504-    opr ^(self, n: ZZ32): String
2505-
2506:    upto(c: Char): String
2507:    beyond(c: Char): String
2508-
2509-    (** The operator %||% with at least one String argument converts to string and
2510-        appends **)

content.content:
(** Indexing by ranges.  The results are 0-based when the
        underlying index type has a notion of 0.  This ensures
        consistency of behavior between types such as vectors that
        ``only'' support 0-indexing and types such as arrays that permit
        other choices of lower bounds.  The easiest way to write the
        index by ranges operation for an instance of %Indexed% is to
        take advantage of indexing on the ranges themselves by writing
        %(bounds())[r]% in order to narrow and bounds check the range %r%
        and obtain a closed range of indices on the underlying
        data. **)
    abstract opr[r:Range[\I\]] : Indexed[\E,I\]
    opr[_:TrivialOpenRange] : Indexed[\E,I\]

    (** Roughly speaking, %ivmap(f)% is equivalent to
        %indexValuePairs.map(f)%.  However %ivmap% is not
        merely a convenient shortcut.  It is actually intended to
        create a copy of the underlying indexed structure when that is
        appropriate.

        or Nothing if no such index exists. **)
    indexOf(e:E): Maybe[\I\]
end

trait ZeroIndexed[\E\] extends Indexed[\E,ZZ32\]
    getter bounds(): CompactFullRange[\ZZ32\]
    abstract opr[r:Range[\ZZ32\]] : ZeroIndexed[\E\]
    zip[\F\](g:ZeroIndexed[\F\]):ZeroIndexed[\(E,F)\]
end

object DefaultZip[\E,F\](e:ZeroIndexed[\E\],f:ZeroIndexed[\F\])

component WrittenReductionArgumentsWalk
import List.{...}
export Executable

(* String's upto and beyond answer the text before and after a character's first occurrence, and List's range subscript answers its elements at strides 1 and 2 as a list of its own element type. *)

lengthOfZZ32s(xs: List[\ZZ32\]): ZZ32 = |xs|

run(): () = do
    assert("abc".upto('b'), "a", "upto of a character that occurs once answers the text before it")
    assert("abc".beyond('b'), "c", "beyond of a character that occurs once answers the text after it")
    assert("hello".upto('l'), "he", "upto of a character that occurs twice answers the text before its first occurrence")
    assert("hello".beyond('l'), "lo", "beyond of a character that occurs twice answers the text after its first occurrence")
    assert("abc".upto('z'), "abc", "upto of a character that does not occur answers the whole string")
    assert("abc".beyond('z'), "", "beyond of a character that does not occur answers the empty string")
    assert("abc".upto('a'), "", "upto of the first character answers the empty string")
    assert("abc".beyond('c'), "", "beyond of the last character answers the empty string")

    l = <|[\ZZ32\] 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 |>
    assert(l[1#3], <|[\ZZ32\] 11, 12, 13 |>, "the list at 1#3, stride 1, is its elements at 1, 2 and 3 (ranges.tex, section \"Ranges\")")
    assert(l[0:4:2], <|[\ZZ32\] 10, 12, 14 |>, "the list at 0:4:2, stride 2, is its elements at 0, 2 and 4, a List[\\ZZ32\\] (ranges.tex, section \"Ranges\"; aggregate.tex, section \"List Expressions\")")
    evens: List[\ZZ32\] = l[0:4:2]
    assert(|evens|, 3, "the list at 0:4:2 binds to a local declared List[\\ZZ32\\]")
    assert(lengthOfZZ32s(l[1:5:2]), 3, "the list at 1:5:2 passes to a parameter declared List[\\ZZ32\\]")
    s = <|[\String\] "p", "q", "r", "s" |>
    assert(s[0#2], <|[\String\] "p", "q" |>, "the list of strings at 0#2, stride 1, is p and q (ranges.tex, section \"Ranges\")")
    assert(s[1:3:2], <|[\String\] "q", "s" |>, "the list of strings at 1:3:2, stride 2, is q and s, a List[\\String\\] (ranges.tex, section \"Ranges\"; aggregate.tex, section \"List Expressions\")")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's checker-count stage: run the bytecode compiler's static checker over the
# INTERPRETER's library, with the interpreter's prelude in scope, and print the per-api
# error table, the total and the crash line that follows it.
#
# Why it exists: POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-21, "the library route" - one library, the
# interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks - and step 1 of
# coordinator/library-route-judgement.md, which makes the distance to that goal a
# permanent gate stage rather than a one-off script. A change in the count is reported, not red (checker-gate-review.md).
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched:
# javac output and the checker's caches go to the scratch directory (default: $TMPDIR
# or /tmp), and the caches are given to the JVM as -Dfortress.caches, honoured through
# ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283, so default_repository/ is never read or written.
# Exit 0 if the table holds a total; 1 if no table could be produced, or if the table holds
# no total because the run's errors are not the checker's (#stopped, below). 20 s in the
# main tree, measured 2026-09-22; it needs no library rebuild and no warm cache.
#
# The run stops after the type checker (WorldFlip -stop check), since 2026-10-24 (climb batch
# 22): the compiler's own phase order up to and including TYPECHECK, integer literal folding
# included, as the distance stage's DistanceMulti -order check. Past the checker, the code
# generator's refusals are not the checker's errors (FACTS F-34 counts them), and its first
# one throws, so a run on a library the checker passes went on into the code generator and
# printed no total. A run the checker stops runs the same phases as before; a clean check,
# a run that reached the component's check and ended rc 0 with no error line, reads as 0.
#

#!/bin/bash
# Compile-path ladder, restricted to the files this rung can affect.
#
# A copy of ../run-ladder.sh with two changes: the ladder root and output
# directory are private to this worktree, and the two whole-corpus loops are
# replaced by one driven by subset.txt (corpus<TAB>file per line).
#
# Pushes every interpreter test program (ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss) and every
# file in ProjectFortress/not_working_library_tests/ through the compiler path
# unchanged and records how far each one gets.
#
# Reproduce:  bash explorations/compile-ladder/run-ladder.sh
# Outputs:    explorations/compile-ladder/raw/<corpus>/<name>.{compile,run}
#             explorations/compile-ladder/results.tsv
#
# The run uses a private cache tree so it never touches default_repository/caches
# (fortress.caches system property + FORTRESS_CACHES env; ProjectProperties.java:283,
# same mechanism the suite uses at build.xml:941-943), and a private java.io.tmpdir
# so the 5.8 MB Rats! temp directory of every grammar-importing run (RatsUtil.java:138-144)
# is swept per file instead of filling the disk.

set -u

source "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../../../explorations/experiment/env.sh"

LADDER_ROOT="${LADDER_ROOT:-$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp/ladder-r1}"
export LADDER_CACHES="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-caches"
export LADDER_TMP="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-tmp"
export FORTRESS_CACHES="$LADDER_CACHES"
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx2g -Xss64m -Dfortress.caches=$LADDER_CACHES -Djava.io.tmpdir=$LADDER_TMP"

PRISTINE="$LADDER_ROOT/pristine"
OUT="$FORTRESS_HOME/explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static"
RAW="$OUT/raw"
TSV="$OUT/results.tsv"

COMPILE_TIMEOUT=120
RUN_TIMEOUT=60
MIN_FREE_KB=512000

mkdir -p "$RAW/tests" "$RAW/not_working_library_tests" "$LADDER_TMP"

disk_guard () {
    local free
    free=$(df -P / | awk 'NR==2{print $4}')
    if [ "$free" -lt "$MIN_FREE_KB" ]; then
        echo "STOP: only ${free} KB free on / (floor ${MIN_FREE_KB} KB)" | tee -a "$OUT/ladder.log"
        exit 2
    fi
    echo "-- disk free ${free} KB, cache $(du -sm "$LADDER_CACHES" | cut -f1) MB"
}

# Source this in every shell that runs Fortress:  source explorations/experiment/env.sh
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64
export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH"
export FORTRESS_HOME="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
export FORTRESS_THREADS=1
# bin/fortress defaults to -Xmx256m (gap ledger row 67); the checks at 4 threads override FORTRESS_THREADS on the command line
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m"
# every grammar-importing run leaves a 5.8 MB Rats! temp directory behind (RatsUtil.getTempDir); 723 of them filled the disk allowance on 2026-09-15.
# Remove only those that no run can still be using: nothing in it written for an hour, and no java process now
# running started before its last write (a run makes its directory after it starts, and reads it until it ends).
(
  oldest=$(ps -C java -o etimes= 2>/dev/null | sort -n | tail -1 | tr -d ' ')
  now=$(date +%s)
  find /tmp -maxdepth 1 -type d -name 'fortress*rats' -mmin +60 -printf '%T@ %p\n' 2>/dev/null |
  while read -r t d ; do
    [ -n "$oldest" ] && [ "${t%.*}" -ge $(( now - oldest )) ] && continue
    [ -n "$(find "$d" -newermt '60 minutes ago' -print -quit 2>/dev/null)" ] && continue
    rm -rf "$d"
  done
)

        timeout 600 ../bin/fortress compile "$f" || { echo "LIBRARY BUILD FAILED on $f"; exit 1; }
    done
}

# Step 2: one known-good compiled program must print PASS before the ladder starts.
sanity () {
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1
    timeout 200 ../bin/fortress compile library_tests/Integer1.fss > /dev/null 2>&1 || return 1
    timeout 60 ../bin/fortress run Integer1 2>&1 | grep -q PASS
}

# Keep only the library's own cache entries; a program's entries are never reused.
prune_cache () {
    ( cd "$LADDER_CACHES" && find . -type f -print ) | sort > "$LADDER_TMP/.now"
    ( cd "$PRISTINE" && find . -type f -print ) | sort > "$LADDER_TMP/.keep"
    comm -23 "$LADDER_TMP/.now" "$LADDER_TMP/.keep" | while read -r p; do
        rm -f "$LADDER_CACHES/$p"
    done
}

component_of () {
    # component/api name as declared, which is what `fortress run` wants
    sed -n 's/^[[:space:]]*\(component\|api\)[[:space:]]\+\([A-Za-z0-9_.]\+\).*/\2/p' "$1" | head -1
}

run_one () {
    local corpus="$1" path="$2"
    local base name comp crc rrc t0 t1 ct rt
    base=$(basename "$path")
    name="${base%.*}"
    comp=$(component_of "$path")
    [ -n "$comp" ] || comp="$name"

    t0=$(date +%s)
    timeout -k 5 "$COMPILE_TIMEOUT" ../bin/fortress compile "$path" \
        > "$RAW/$corpus/$base.compile" 2>&1
    crc=$?
    t1=$(date +%s); ct=$((t1-t0))

    rrc=""
    rt=""
    if [ "$crc" -eq 0 ] && [ "${base##*.}" = "fss" ]; then
        t0=$(date +%s)
        timeout -k 5 "$RUN_TIMEOUT" ../bin/fortress run "$comp" \
            > "$RAW/$corpus/$base.run" 2>&1
        rrc=$?
        t1=$(date +%s); rt=$((t1-t0))
    fi

    printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' \
        "$corpus" "$base" "$comp" "$crc" "$rrc" "$ct" "$rt" >> "$TSV"
    echo "$corpus/$base crc=$crc rrc=$rrc ${ct}s"
}

main () {
    echo "=== ladder start $(date -Is) ==="
    disk_guard
    if [ ! -d "$PRISTINE" ]; then
        build_library
        rm -rf "$PRISTINE"; cp -a "$LADDER_CACHES" "$PRISTINE"
    fi
    sanity || { echo "SANITY FAILED: library_tests/Integer1 did not print PASS"; exit 1; }
    echo "sanity ok: library_tests/Integer1 compiles and prints PASS"
    prune_cache

    : > "$TSV"
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1

    local n=0 line corpus f
    while IFS=$'\t' read -r corpus f; do
        [ -n "$corpus" ] || continue
        run_one "$corpus" "$corpus/$f"
        n=$((n+1))
        rm -rf "${LADDER_TMP:?}"/fortress*rats
        if [ $((n % 10)) -eq 0 ]; then prune_cache; disk_guard; fi
    done < "$OUT/subset.txt"
    prune_cache
    echo "=== ladder done $(date -Is), $n files ==="
    disk_guard
}

#!/bin/bash
# The distance stage's comparison: this table (run.sh's) against the last landed one.
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/compare.sh <last-landed-table|""> <this-table>
#
# Prints one verdict line, then every #kind and #class row whose count moved, with the
# change, and every #crash row that went or came. It is REPORTED and never red: it always
# exits 0, whatever moved, a stale shadow and a run that produced no table included (Pavol,
# answer 11, POSITIONS.md 2026-09-26: a report-only stage, whose job is driving the distance
# down). The verdicts:
#   DISTANCE DOWN|UP|SAME   <last> -> <now>
#   DISTANCE FIRST          no landed table to compare with
#   DISTANCE NO TABLE       this run produced no count, with the table's own reason
#   SETTING CHANGED         the two tables ran different settings: the counts are not like for like
#   SHADOW STALE            a shadow edit no longer matches the tracked sources
# A move of 2 to 4 errors in the components' type errors or in which pair of LEXICO, SQCAP or
# INVERSE declarations an overloading error names is the checker's run-to-run variation
# (switch-over-distance-flat.md section 5), not a change; a crash row whose line numbers
# moved because a rung edited above it prints as one gone and one new.

DISTANCE DOWN   5 -> 1 (-4)
    kind typecheck                4 -> 0      (-4)
    class BR                      2 -> 0      (-2)  big operators: a reduction's body typed as the element, not the BigReduction or Comprehension declared
    class OT                      2 -> 0      (-2)  other body errors (one-off library slips and checker limits)
    unit component FortressLibrary      4 -> 1      (-3)
    unit component List           1 -> 0      (-1)
rc=0

content.content:
== explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:7-27

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

              (outer:BigOperator[\I0,O0,R0,L0\],

        (outer'.unwrap)(gg'.generate2[\I0,L0,L1\](o, i, fn x => (inner'.body)(innerBody(x))))

            o.lift((resolvedouterBody)(((inner.unwrap)(i.unlift(

\subsection{Reductions whose element type nothing fixes}
\seclabel{revival-reductions}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] \secref{reduction-expr}.
\item[Change] One box after the first sentence says that neither implementation
directs the desugaring of a reduction by type yet, so a reduction with a
generator clause list whose element type no argument fixes writes its static
argument; and that until the compiled path is built on the libraries this
specification describes, it compiles against a smaller library of its own,
whose big operators take no static argument and range over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}
only, so that there the clause form runs without its static argument and a
written one is refused. The normative text is unchanged.
The box said at first that ``the interpreter, and the compiled type checker
when it checks the libraries this specification describes, each take
\TYP{BottomType} for it, and the reduction then accepts no element''; it now
says that the interpreter does, and that the compiled type checker takes the
bound of the big operator's static parameter, which gives the reduction the
type of a bound such as \TYP{Number} and no instance that applies where the
bound mentions the static parameter itself.
A revision of the interpreter of 9~October 2026 changes the box once more.
It said that ``When no argument of the big operator fixes the element type, the
interpreter takes \TYP{BottomType} for it, and the reduction then accepts no
element''; it now says that where the bound of the big operator's static
parameter mentions the static parameter itself the interpreter leaves that
parameter open and the reduction runs on the types of its elements, an empty
one taking the identity of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and that until the compiled
type checker directs the desugaring by type a program that both implementations
are to run writes the static argument.
A revision of the interpreter of 14~October 2026 changes the box once more.
It said that ``Neither implementation directs it by type yet'', and that where
the bound of the big operator's static parameter mentions the static parameter
itself ``the interpreter leaves that parameter open'', the reduction running on
the types of its elements ``except that an empty one takes the identity of
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} whatever the type of the expression''; it now says that
neither implementation directs it by the type \VAR{N} of the expression yet,
that the interpreter, which has no static types, instantiates the big operator
by the declared type of the local variable, or the declared return type of the
top-level or local function, whose value the reduction is, otherwise by the
join of the run-time types of its elements, and where
there is none at the bound of its static parameter, or open where that bound
mentions the parameter itself, and that an empty reduction that no declared
type directs takes the identity of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}.
\item[Rationale] The revival decided on 26~September 2026 that the library's
\OPR{SUM} and \OPR{PROD} become generic reductions over the library's algebra,
each joined with its element type's own operator and taking that type's
identity, and that such a clause form writes its static argument, as the team's
own tests do.
Until 9~October 2026 the interpreter took \TYP{BottomType} for the static
parameter of a big operator that no argument fixes (row~424 of the revival's
gap ledger).
The revival decided on 8~October 2026 that the interpreter leaves open a type
parameter whose bound mentions the type parameter itself and that nothing at a
call fixes (\secref{revival-inference}): having no static types, the
interpreter cannot take the type \VAR{N} of the expression, and an open
parameter refuses no element where \TYP{BottomType} refused every one, so that
the reduction runs on the types of its elements, as the desugaring by type
would run it.
Reversing that revision takes one block out of the interpreter's
instantiation of a call and returns such a parameter to \TYP{BottomType}; the
specification's examples that write no static argument for such a reduction
would stop again at their first element, and refusing the call, as the compiled
type checker does, would stop them too.
The revival decided on 14~October 2026 that the interpreter instantiates the
big operator of a reduction or a comprehension that writes no static argument
as the desugaring by the type \VAR{N} would, with run-time types in place of
\VAR{N}: by the declared type of the local variable, or the declared return
type of the top-level or local function, whose value the reduction is, which
constrains the instance as a call's static return type
does (\secref{static-arg-inference}), and otherwise by the join of the
run-time types of its elements, which the interpreter collects before it
reduces them, as it already took the types of the elements for \VAR{N} where
it left the parameter open; with neither, the parameter takes its bound, or is
left open where the bound mentions it.
Until then the interpreter left a big operator's static parameter whose bound
does not mention it at \TYP{BottomType} (\secref{revival-inference}), and an
empty reduction, having no element, took the identity of
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}.
Reversing the revision of 14~October 2026 takes the declared type and the

content.content:
reproducer   one test (a name under the test folders, or a path) or probe
               path from the repository root, or `none`
  limits       row 1,200 characters, claim 300, reproducer 200, found by 60,
               notes 700
  a pipe inside a cell is written \\|

Cells are split only at a pipe that is not escaped as \\|. A row whose cells
hold bare pipes (the ledger had six) does not split into its table's width that
way; it is read by its split at pipes followed by a space or the line's end, as
facts-extract.py has always read it, and check reports it under `pipe`.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .ledger.lock beside the ledger), checks the
template on the line it writes, and puts the full earlier line of a row it
changes, unchanged, in the history file beside the ledger
(fortress-gap-ledger-history.md), under "### Row N" and a line saying what
became of it. A failed check prints the rules the row breaks and exits 1.
add, rewrite, close and duplicate check the whole line they write; note checks
only what it changes (the notes cell and the row's length), so that a row
failing the template elsewhere still takes a note. A row at its length limit
takes no note: rewrite cuts it back (the rework's decision D4, "each is cut
when next edited", process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md).

usage: ledger.py COMMAND [ARGS] [--root DIR] [--ledger FILE] [--history FILE]

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the
                             paths the row cites in backticks
  sections                   each section that holds a row table: its row
                             count and title, tab-separated
  section TITLE              the heads of that section's rows
  show N [--short]           row N under its section and table header; with
                             --short, its status, class, claim and the notes'
                             first 300 characters
  find WORDS [--open] [--cites FILE[:LINE]] [--all]
                             one line per row that holds every word (whole
                             words, or a word's start with a trailing *):
                             number, status, class, the claim's start; --open
                             leaves out FIXED, DUPLICATE and RETIRED; --cites
                             keeps the rows citing FILE (at LINE) and prints
                             the lines they cite; at most 10 rows unless --all
  count                      the rows by status, kind and area; nothing stored
  add FILE --section TITLE   FILE holds one row line, its # cell `?` (or the
                             seven cells after it); numbers it max + 1 and
                             inserts it in that section's table in number
                             order
  note N TEXT                adds TEXT to row N's notes, before the row's own
                             "full text: history, row N" marker where it has
                             one, else at their end (notes of `none` are
                             replaced); checks the notes cell and the row's
                             length only, so a failure in another cell does
                             not block it; a row keeps its own cells
  rewrite N FILE             FILE holds row N's whole new line (its # cell N
                             or ?, or the seven cells after it); checks it
                             against the template and writes it in the row's
                             place, its earlier line in the history
                             ("rewritten"): the route that corrects a claim,
                             cuts notes, or moves a reproducer. A FIXED or
                             DUPLICATE row stays so (a FIXED row's commit is
                             checked); a row becomes one only by close or
                             duplicate
  close N --commit HASH --test NAME [--settled TEXT] [--note TEXT] [--claim C]
